stories.dek: ‘A nation’s military power is as good as its industrial power,’ said Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) General N.S.

Chief of Defence Staff of the Indian Armed Forces Gen. N. S. Raja Subramani. File | Photo Credit: AP

The distinction between war and peace is blurring, with nations facing a continuous state of contestation, Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) General N.S. Raja Subramani said on Friday (November 27, 2026), underscoring the need for India to strengthen its military capabilities across domains, including electronic and cognitive warfare.

Addressing a lecture on the ‘Future of Warfare and India’s Preparedness to Conduct Multi-Domain Operations’ organised by the Vivekananda International Foundation (VIF) in New Delhi, Gen. Subramani said adversaries were subjecting India to cognitive warfare in an insidious manner. He said efforts were underway to modernise the electronic warfare architecture of the armed forces.

While the nature of war remained fundamentally unchanged as a contest of political will, political objectives and human will, its character was evolving rapidly, driven predominantly by technology, he said. Technology was reshaping military architecture and accelerating the pace of decision-making, he added.

Drawing lessons from recent conflicts, the CDS cited the Armenia-Azerbaijan war to highlight the growing role of drones and loitering munitions, the Israel-Hamas conflict to underline the importance of surprise and deception, and the US-Israel-Iran conflict for the increasing significance of long-range strikes and artificial intelligence-enabled decision-making.

Emphasising the link between military and industrial capabilities, he said, “A nation’s military power is as good as its industrial power.”

Reflecting on the lessons of Operation Sindoor, Gen. Subramani described its second phase as an excellent example of joint, integrated and multi-domain operations. He asserted that India had control over the escalation matrix and escalation dominance during the operation, which resulted in a “decisive victory” for the country.

He highlighted the importance of political-military coordination, intelligence, joint planning and integration among the three Services. The operation demonstrated the effectiveness of precise, intelligence-led strikes by the Army and the Navy without collateral damage, besides the successful employment of indigenous long-range strike capabilities such as BrahMos, he said.

stories.title: Israeli strikes kill 16 schoolchildren so far this month, Gaza ministry says
stories.dek: Statement follows death of sisters, aged 15 and 13, in airstrike on residential apartment in Gaza City Israeli strikes have killed at least 16 schoolchildren in Gaza since the start of November, as yo…
stories.content:
Palestinians mourn Mohammed Majed Abu Al-Awf, 47, his wife, Noura Ezzat Abu Al-Awf, 41, and their daughters, Yusra, 15, and Jana, 13, who were killed in an Israeli airstrike on their home in western Gaza City. Photograph: Mohammed M Skaik/JNA/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Palestinians mourn Mohammed Majed Abu Al-Awf, 47, his wife, Noura Ezzat Abu Al-Awf, 41, and their daughters, Yusra, 15, and Jana, 13, who were killed in an Israeli airstrike on their home in western Gaza City. Photograph: Mohammed M Skaik/JNA/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock Gaza Israeli strikes kill 16 schoolchildren so far this month, Gaza ministry says Statement follows death of sisters, aged 15 and 13, in airstrike on residential apartment in Gaza City

Israeli strikes have killed at least 16 schoolchildren in Gaza since the start of November, as young people across the territory face intensifying bombardment and a struggle to find food, clean water and shelter.

On Wednesday, Gaza’s ministry of education said: “Palestinian students had been targeted for the third time in less than 24 hours, in an escalation reflecting the continued Israeli violations against children in the Gaza Strip. The number of schoolchildren killed since the beginning of November has now risen to 16.”

The statement follows the death of two sisters, Yusra, 15, and Jana Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 13, in the early hours of Wednesday in an airstrike targeting a residential apartment in western Gaza City.

Yusra was a pupil at Kafr Qasim school, while her sister Jana attended al-Manar private school.

The ministry added: “The girls’ father, Mohammed Majed Abu Al-Ouf, and their mother, Noura Ezzat Abu Al-Ouf, were also killed in the strike which injured several other Palestinians.” The father was a director of internal security services for Hamas in northern Gaza.

Earlier this year, an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.

View image in fullscreen Palestinian children outside a residential block hit by Israeli strikes in Gaza City in 2025. Photograph: Ebrahim Hajjaj/Reuters On 6 November, Mohammed Nidal Barbakh, 15, was shot by Israeli forces in the Bir 19 area of al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, and later died from his injuries.

He was in the 10th grade at the Muscat school and dreamed of becoming a professional football player.

stories.title: Iranian state media releases AI video threatening attacks on Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX headquarters
stories.dek: The video singles out the companies for supporting the military campaign against Iran.
stories.content:
Iranian state media released a chilling AI-generated video threatening attacks on the headquarters of Amazon, Microsoft and Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

The video, posted Thursday on Telegram by the Islamic Republic’s Mehr News agency, shows a terror group launching drone strikes on the tech giants as explosions and flames engulf their headquarters.

“We won’t let the killers of our children off the hook,” the narrator declares in English.

“We will not harm the American people,” the voice adds. “Consider this a warning.”

The video singles out the companies for supporting the war on Iran , which began in February.

“The companies that took part in the attack on Iran will either pay reparations and repent or face destruction on the same scale,” the narrator says as images of burning buildings flash across the screen.

“Repentance or destruction? The choice is yours, America,” the video finishes.

The Telegram post accompanying the video also condemned the February bombing of an elementary school in Minab , where a preliminary military investigation determined the US was responsible for a missile strike that killed 175 people, most of them children.

“A stern warning to companies complicit in crimes against the Iranian people and the innocent children of Minab!” the post read.

“From Amazon to Microsoft, companies that have secret collaborations with US and Israeli military units cannot escape accountability.”

The threats come as President Trump’s war effort faces an uncertain future.

In an exclusive Oval Office interview with The Post this week, Trump revealed the military campaign is funded through January and warned that Democrats could undermine the US effort if they take control of Congress.

“I mean, if they do that, look their navy’s gone, their air force is gone, their anti-aircraft, everything’s gone. Their leaders are gone. I mean, if [Democrats] do that, they’ll just take a win and make it a loss.”

“I don’t know how they could do that politically, because we have a win. We can put that war to bed anytime we want,” he added.

stories.title: The M5 MacBook Air just got its biggest discount since Apple raised the price
stories.dek: If you’ve been holding off on buying a new MacBook Air since Apple raised prices by $200 in June, you’re in luck.
stories.content:
The new promo drops Apple’s 13-incher to within $100 of its all-time low, easing the sting of recent price hikes.

The new promo drops Apple’s 13-incher to within $100 of its all-time low, easing the sting of recent price hikes.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

If you’ve been holding off on buying a new MacBook Air since Apple raised prices by $200 in June , you’re in luck. The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air is on sale at Amazon and Best Buy with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage starting at $999 ($300 off) for Black Friday, which is the lowest price we’ve seen since the hike. If you want a larger display, Amazon and Best Buy are also taking $300 off the otherwise identical 15-inch model with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, dropping it to $1,199.

The M5-equipped MacBook Air is a good middle ground if you need more power than the MacBook Neo — which, thanks to a $100 discount , is $599 — but don’t want to splurge on a MacBook Pro. Its faster chip, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage make it better suited for multitasking and creative work in apps like Photoshop and Premiere. You also get a higher-resolution display, better speakers, a backlit keyboard that makes typing in the dark easier, and faster ports. Plus, its sharper webcam supports Apple’s Center Stage feature, which automatically adjusts the framing to keep you in view during video calls.

Of course, the Air can’t match the performance or higher-end displays you can get with a MacBook Pro, whether you opt for an M5 model , the newer M5 Pro model with a PROLED XDR Display , or one of the M6-powered machines . A Pro may be worth the extra money if you regularly edit video or work on more demanding creative projects. But if you mostly need a laptop for work, browsing, and occasional photo or video editing, the M5 Air is more than capable.

stories.title: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution
stories.dek: Scientists have discovered a faster way to identify diamond-based materials that could power quantum computers and sensors at room temperature.
stories.content:
A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

This capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

stories.title: Eastern Mediterranean Maritime Agreements and Regional Energy Corridors
stories.dek: A multi-perspective assessment of offshore natural gas transit frameworks, maritime boundary negotiations, and regional stability.
stories.content:
The Eastern Mediterranean basin continues to navigate complex multilateral diplomatic engagements balancing offshore energy exploration with sovereign boundary delimitation. High-level delegations from regional coastal states and European partners are refining frameworks that align pipeline routes with equitable maritime economic zones.

Key Perspectives & Strategic Dimensions:
1. Energy Transit Security: Multilateral agreements between Mediterranean states prioritize uninterrupted transit of natural gas to Southern European ports, diversifying continental supply lines.
2. Maritime Boundary Delimitation: Diplomatic mediators emphasize that long-term maritime stability necessitates transparent dispute-resolution mechanisms that account for sovereign continental shelf claims.
3. Regional Economic Interdependence: Joint infrastructure investments in subsea interconnectors create economic mutual interest, offering pragmatic stabilization incentives across diverse stakeholders.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly impacts the economic stability, energy infrastructure, and security landscape across the Levant and Mediterranean.

stories.title: Sub-Microsecond Spin Dynamics in Diamond NV Centers: Benchmarking Cavity QED and Coherence Limits
stories.dek: Mitigating dipolar spin-spin dephasing and hyperfine bath interactions in dense diamond NV ensembles via Floquet driving.
stories.content:
Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) color centers in diamond remain the preeminent solid-state platform for room-temperature quantum metrology and nanoscale magnetic resonance. Scaling from isolated defects to dense ensembles requires overcoming collective dephasing from the surrounding 13C nuclear spin bath.

Recent breakthroughs utilizing microwave cavity coupling and Floquet dynamical decoupling extend the effective coherence time (T2*) by an order of magnitude.

Key Technical Highlights:
1. Cooperative Purcell Enhancement: Dense NV ensembles entering the collective strong coupling regime demonstrate cavity-mediated coherence preservation.
2. Suppression of Spin-Diffusion Loss: Operating within crystallographic symmetry subspaces eliminates cross-axis relaxation.
3. Room-Temperature Sensing: Sustained microsecond coherence enables sub-picotesla magnetic field sensitivities for single-cell NMR.
stories.whyItMatters: Informs room-temperature diamond quantum magnetometry, microwave cavity loading, and advanced Floquet decoupling protocols in spin dynamics.

stories.source: Innatera & Edge AI Insights • 5 min read
stories.title: Sub-Milliwatt Neuromorphic Microcontrollers Shift Real-Time AI Inference to the Edge
stories.dek: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) on silicon processors achieve microsecond response times at sub-milliwatt power budgets.
stories.content:
The paradigm of routing sensor telemetry to centralized cloud servers is rapidly transitioning to on-device neuromorphic microcontrollers. Utilizing event-driven spiking neural architectures, silicon accelerators process acoustic and vibration patterns with near-zero latency.

Key Highlights:
1. In-Memory Processing: Spiking architectures circumvent the classical von Neumann memory bottleneck, consuming less than 1 mW.
2. Zero Cloud Exposure: Sensitive sensor streams remain strictly local, guaranteeing privacy and continuous operation during network blackouts.
3. Predictive Maintenance: Deployed microcontrollers classify industrial vibrations and structural stress in real time.
stories.whyItMatters: Enables zero-latency, private, on-device anomaly detection and vibration monitoring without cloud roundtrips.

stories.title: Circadian Photonic Priming and Equanimity in Demanding Research
stories.dek: Aligning 90-minute ultradian deep work blocks with natural circadian rhythms and secular Buddhist non-reactivity.
stories.content:
Sustained high-level analytical performance requires deliberate biological pacing. Structuring the day around 90-minute ultradian cycles followed by brief decompression intervals prevents cognitive fatigue.

Core Evidence-Based Habits:
1. Photonic Lock: Direct outdoor light exposure within 45 minutes of waking aligns the suprachiasmatic nucleus master clock.
2. Ultradian Block: Dedicate the primary 9:00 AM - 10:30 AM window to pure theoretical derivation before checking correspondence.
3. Secular Equanimity (Dhammapada 81): 'Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.'
stories.whyItMatters: Protects cognitive bandwidth and prevents attentional fragmentation during demanding laboratory derivations.

papers.title: Nitrogen-Vacancy Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy of $^{15}$N Spins in Potassium Nitrite Solution
papers.authors: Sehrish Iqbal, Jitender Kumar, Suvechhya Lamichhane et al.
papers.tldr: Nitrogen is essential in agricultural fertilizers, yet its nanoscale interfacial dynamics remain largely unexplored. Although quadrupolar broadening complicates $^{14}$N nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) detection, $^{15}$N (I=1/2) provides well-defined nuclear-spin signatures but remains challenging to detect at the nanoscale due to its low natural abundance and small gyromagnetic ratio.
takeaways: Although quadrupolar broadening complicates $^{14}$N nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) detection, $^{15}$N (I=1/2) provides well-defined nuclear-spin signatures but remains challenging to detect at the nanoscale due to its low natural abundance and small gyromagnetic ratio.

Here, we use a microfluidic quantum sensing platform based on shallow nitrogen vacancy (NV) centers in diamond to detect $^{15}$N NMR from KNO$_{3}$ solution at room temperature and in a low magnetic field regime.
This is consistent with the formation of a KNO$_{3}$ adsorption layer on the diamond surface, supported by surface characterization.

papers.title: Phonon-Aware Electron-to-Nuclear Spin Quantum Memory in NV Centers
papers.tldr: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond are a promising solid-state platform for quantum memory: the electron spin can be optically initialized and read out, while nearby nuclear spins have long coherence times and can serve as storage qubits. In this work, we develop a phonon-aware open quantum system model for electron-to-nuclear spin state transfer in a single NV center.
takeaways: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond are a promising solid-state platform for quantum memory: the electron spin can be optically initialized and read out, while nearby nuclear spins have long coherence times and can serve as storage qubits.
In this work, we develop a phonon-aware open quantum system model for electron-to-nuclear spin state transfer in a single NV center.

With the default decoherence rates, increasing the spin-phonon coupling from 0 to 0.06 MHz lowers the worst-case retrieval fidelity from 0.9994 to 0.9884, and the fidelity oscillates with the phonon-mode period because electron-phonon entanglement generated during the write step is partially undone during the read step.

papers.title: Infrared-absorption magnetometry in a diamond nanocavity: demonstration and limits at the nanoscale
papers.authors: Nicholas J. Sorensen, Elham Zohari, Chris Coutts et al.
papers.tldr: Diamond quantum sensors promise both high spatial resolution and high sensitivity; however, conventional photoluminescence-based spin readout can be difficult to integrate efficiently. Infrared absorption by nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond provides a promising alternative, although the sensitivity of compact absorption-based sensors is limited by the short optical interaction length between the probe field and the NV ensemble.
takeaways: Diamond quantum sensors promise both high spatial resolution and high sensitivity; however, conventional photoluminescence-based spin readout can be difficult to integrate efficiently.

Infrared absorption by nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond provides a promising alternative, although the sensitivity of compact absorption-based sensors is limited by the short optical interaction length between the probe field and the NV ensemble.
To overcome this limitation, we demonstrate, for the first time, singlet-absorption magnetometry using spin-dense diamond nanocavities.

papers.title: Systematically improvable semiclassical clustering for accurate and efficient quantum dynamics in large spin ensembles
papers.tldr: Predicting the decoherence of spin qubits in realistic environments is key to identifying the interactions that limit their coherence---a prerequisite for designing better quantum technologies. While accurate methods for spin dynamics are limited to relatively small systems, the dissipative spin environments in real experiments typically involve orders of magnitude more spins.
takeaways: Predicting the decoherence of spin qubits in realistic environments is key to identifying the interactions that limit their coherence---a prerequisite for designing better quantum technologies.
We show that our method is applicable to systems containing arbitrary spin species under dynamical decoupling pulse sequences.

We demonstrate that cluster spin-LSC recovers numerically exact coherence and population dynamics for a nitrogen-vacancy center and a molecular qubit, reducing day-long multi-GPU simulations to only minutes on a CPU.

papers.title: Signatures of Kitaev quantum spin liquid states in $α$-RuCl$_3$ revealed by nitrogen-vacancy spin-noise spectroscopy
papers.authors: Jitender Kumar, Sehrish Iqbal, Himani Saraswat et al.
papers.tldr: Bond-dependent magnetic interactions, strong spin-orbit coupling, and quantum fluctuations in $α$-RuCl$_3$ make it an archetypical candidate for exotic Kitaev quantum spin liquid (QSL) states. While electronic transport, neutron scattering, optical and tunneling spectroscopies were used to probe global QSL signatures in large scale $α$-RuCl$_3$ samples, nanoscale evidence of local QSL behavior via a non-invasive experimental probe is still missing.
takeaways: Here, we use diamond nitrogen-vacancy (NV) spin-noise spectroscopy to probe QSL states in α-RuCl3 nanoflakes with thicknesses ranging from 8 to 150 nm over a temperature range of 4.3-250 K.

Our measurements reveal a pronounced decrease in the NV spin-lattice relaxation time ($T_{1}$) below ~100 K in proximity to the $α$-RuCl$_3$ flakes, indicating enhanced GHz-frequency magnetic fluctuations.

These results establish NV spin-noise spectroscopy as a local, non-invasive probe of low-energy spin dynamics in $α$-RuCl$_3$ nanoflakes and open a route to testing predicted noise signatures of fractionalized excitations in atomically thin QSL candidates.
